newsitem.title: UK: UK's Cook to meet EU over Hong Kong.
newsitem.headline: UK's Cook to meet EU over Hong Kong.

text.p: Foreign Secretary Robin Cook will tell the European Union on Thursday why British ministers plan to boycott the swearing in of a new Hong Kong legislature, but officials said he would not plead with the EU to follow suit.
Although Britain will stage a ministerial boycott of the ceremony, senior British officials will, however, attend.
Media reports said Cook would urge his partners to follow Britain's lead when he saw them at the one-day Luxembourg meeting but a senior official said this approach would be too risky.
"I don't think it would help the people of Hong Kong to run a high-profile campaign which didn't work," said the official, who asked to remain nameless.
"I don't think this is the time to start throwing pebbles at the Germans or the French."
Britain and the United States will not send ministers to the July 1 ceremony but many other nations -- including China's major trading partners -- have made it clear they will attend.
Britain on Wednesday said two of its senior officials would be at the swearing in of Beijing's hand-picked provisional legislature but denied it was softening its position.
Britain and the United States firmly oppose the provisional legislature, which will replace the colony's democratically elected parliament. The U.S. consul to Hong Kong will attend the ceremony.
Hong Kong's pro-democracy camp attacked both countries for not boycotting the event, but Cook stressed that Britain had no intention of abandoning the colony.
Cook, speaking to reporters on Wednesday, said Hong Kong citizens could rest assured that Britain would do all it could to defend their interests.

He said he was pleased that recent summits of EU leaders and the G7 group of industrialised nations had stressed to Beijing that it should stick to plans to hold fresh elections to a new Hong Kong legislature within the next 12 months.
He attempted to dismiss speculation that Britain would want to concentrate on boosting trade ties with China once Hong Kong had been handed back.
There will be no facile choice for Britain between Hong Kong and China. We do not have a policy of sacrificing Hong Kong for China, Cook said.
He also said the world community should not be put off by the usual Chinese response to criticism about its Hong Kong policies -- that what happened there was a purely domestic affair.

"China will say Hong Kong is an internal affair every time someone says something and its important we dont say 'Ah yes, we hadnt thought about that. We should be prepared for these statements," he said.
Britain also had no plans to cut the access to ministers and officials which pro-democracy activists like Martin Lee currently enjoy.
"Anyone who speaks for a significant part of Hong Kong opinion will have access and that includes Martin Lee," Cook said.
